title: The mother who stood
hookLine: Mary, who stood at the cross, as comforter of the afflicted
carry: mary comforts because she stood at the cross

lines: HEALTH OF THE SICK, REFUGE OF SINNERS.
cards: A hospital corridor, late at night. Someone has just had bad news, and a friend sits down beside them. The friend doesn't explain anything or fix anything.
Fetches a coffee, sits back down, and stays. Further down the Litany of Loreto, after the towers and the gold, the titles change their tone. Health of the sick.
Refuge of sinners. Comforter of the afflicted. Help of Christians.
The poetry comes down to the ground. Today's word is the one in the middle.

teach.b: In the litany's Latin it's consolatrix afflictorum: the one who consoles the afflicted, the people weighed down. The reason begins with Mary's own grief.
When she brings her baby to the Temple, an old man named Simeon takes him in his arms and then turns to her. In the Douay-Rheims he says: "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce."
The comforter in this title is not someone who was spared. Then the cross.
John's Gospel names who was there, and it starts with her: "Now there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother." No speech. No miracle.
She stood. Some Catholics find in that one verb a whole way of comforting: you don't leave, even when there's nothing to say. Then Paul adds a third turn.
Writing to the church in Corinth, he says God comforts people in all their trouble so that they can comfort others in theirs, with the same comfort they were given.
Comfort, for Paul, travels: received, then handed on.

teach.h: A JOB ANYONE CAN TAKE A SHIFT IN.
teach.b: That's how Catholics hear this title.

teach.h: NOW THERE STOOD BY THE CROSS OF JESUS, HIS MOTHER.
teach.b: Mary, who knew the sword and stood at the cross, passes on the comfort she received, and when they pray comforter of the afflicted, pray for us, they bring her the people who are going under.
And the title quietly describes a job. Anyone can take a shift: the friend in the corridor, the neighbor with a casserole, the text that says I'm here and asks nothing back.

how: Catholics call on Mary as Comforter of the Afflicted in the Litany of Loreto, and parishes and hospital chaplains often bring the title to people who are sick or grieving, alongside visits and practical help.

games.q: what does “comfort of the afflicted” mean?
o: the Latin name of a saint who ran hospitals
a prayer said only at a hospital bedside
a title for Mary, who consoles people weighed down

games.q: comfort of the afflicted — tap the pairs.
p: a sword shall pierce thy soul
his mother stood by the cross

s: at the cross, John's Gospel gives Mary a speech
the text says she stood there. no words, no miracle: she stayed.
Simeon warned Mary of her own sorrow
"and thy own soul a sword shall pierce" (Luke 2:35).
in the litany, the titles of mercy follow the titles of poetry
after morning star come health of the sick, refuge of sinners, comforter of the afflicted and help of Christians.

games.q: a friend has just had terrible news, and there's nothing you can fix. what does the scene at the cross suggest?
o: explain why it might have happened.
stay close, even with nothing to say.
give them space and check in next month.
games.why: John 19:25 gives Mary no words at the cross. it says she stood there. some Catholics find a way of comforting in that one verb.

practice: Let one person come to mind who's carrying something heavy right now, an illness, a loss, a worry they keep mentioning, and stay with them for a few breaths, the way the friend stays in the corridor, without planning any advice.
If you pray, name them and add the litany's line, comforter of the afflicted, pray for us; if you don't, simply hold them.
And if the heavy thing is yours and it feels like too much, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Comfort of the afflicted. In Latin, consolatrix afflictorum: a title of Mary, who knew the sword and stood at the cross, for everyone who is weighed down.

orig.note: Latin: comforter of the afflicted, the title as the Litany of Loreto says it.

carryVoice: Your line: Mary comforts because she stood at the cross. Sometimes comfort is simply staying. I'm glad you came today.
